reason: Depth and thickness of bark are both real traits. The examples are mixed: 'deep' for furrows or fissures, 'thick' for the bark itself, and a bare length. A rule would need to read 'thick' as thickness and 'deep' as the depth of fissures (a different bearer).
Drupelets (fruitlets of Rubus) can be glabrous or hairy. The examples are correct.

The part is the orchid labellum. The examples are 'recurved' or 'reflexed', which is a curvature value, not just 'orientation'. The pair is fine only if a rule maps recurved and reflexed to a curvature or orientation value term. Otherwise it is too generic.
Inflorescence (scape) bracts can be erect.
PATO 'recurrent' means occurring again. In the examples it describes a vein pattern ('recurrent venation'), which is a venation pattern or the course of the veins, not a quality of a vascular bundle.
The examples describe the leaf apex or acumen tapering. The trichome bearer is a wrong reading, probably through 'apex' or 'acumen'.

The examples are pitchers (Nepenthes), where the pitcher is a modified leaf, and ellipsoid is only for part of it ('lower half'). Prolate is the wrong shape term. Ellipsoid belongs on the pitcher, a more specific bearer than 'vascular leaf'. Needs a pitcher class.
The examples are pitchers constricted at a position along the pitcher, not the whole leaf. The bearer is too generic. Re-annotate once there is a pitcher bearer.
Rhizome scales can have a colour. The examples are colour words, correctly annotated.
The examples are 'beak of the perigynium very short' and 'short-stipitate', so the short thing is the beak or stipe, not the perigynium. The wrong part is the bearer.
'Buff' is a pale yellowish-brown, so the PATO term 'orange yellow' is an approximation. Bark colour itself is fine. A rule would need a colour mapping for buff, ideally to a FLOPO colour value term.

Foliage is a diffuse bearer, but hairiness of foliage is meaningful. The PATO term 'pilosity' is the attribute, while the examples give specific values (glabrous, pilose, puberulent, hirsute). Allowed if the value terms are used, not the attribute alone.
Spine shields (Cactaceae) have a 2-D shape, and triangular is correct.

The examples are margins that are crenulate or crenate. The margin is the bearer, not the involucre, and 'scalloped' is only a rough match for crenulate. A rule would need to move this to the margin and use a crenate or crenulate term.
Leaf sheaths can be round or suborbicular in outline (e.g. in some sedges and Eriocaulaceae).
The gynostemium (orchid column) can be coiled or spiral. The examples are correct.
A perigynium can be firm in texture, as in the Carex descriptions.
The examples are the spacing of the pedicel scars along the axis, so the pattern belongs to the arrangement of the scars, not to a single scar. This is a rule for spacing, not a quality of each scar.
A calyptra of a moss capsule can be small.
Capsules can be sessile.
Elaters can have a colour, and the examples are colour words.
Leaf teeth can be large.
Short shoots are a real shoot type, and shoots can be short or abbreviated.

The 'adaxially hairy' examples refer to the hairy petal surface, which an adaxial epidermis can carry. This is acceptable if the rule treats 'adaxially' as part of the bearer. The anterior petal of one example is a different case.
Achenes can be tomentose.
The examples say the bract apex or tip is blunt, not the whole bract. Allowed only if the bearer is moved to the apex.
Terminal capsule (position on the axis) is meaningful in some mosses and in some taxa. A rule would need to read 'terminal' as position of the fruit on the plant, not a trait of the capsule itself.
The single example is 'cupulate' with no clear subject. Cupulate describes the whole corona, not a corona lobe.

The examples are relations to other organs (appressed to column, included in corolla). It depends on what the lobe is attached to. A rule would need a relational pattern, not a plain position quality.
The examples mix a 4-angled stem or fruit ('tetragonous'), a subsquare sepal and subquadrangular lobes. Only the sepal-shape cases are right. A rule would need to separate shape from angularity.
Involucral bracts can be thickened or thick. The base or margin cases should ideally be moved to those parts.
'Entire' in the examples refers to the margin of the auricle, not the auricle itself, and the PATO term may not mean an entire margin. The bearer should be the margin.
A leaf lamina can be lance-ovate.
Rhizomes can be contorted or twisted.
A perianth or its parts can be deciduous or caducous.
Involucral bracts can be striate (with fine lines).
Staminodes can be inconspicuous.
A stigma can be oblate, wider than high.
A leaf sheath can be flat. The 'flat spines' example is a different part and should be checked.
A perigynium can be distended (Carex).
Seeds can be iridescent.
The colour pattern (dotted, streaked) is meaningful on leaf sheaths. The PATO term is a generic attribute, and the specific pattern would need to be a spotted or streaked value.
A peduncle can be viscid (sticky).
An inflorescence can be columnar in form.
The examples say 'subentire' for a stigma margin, which means almost entire. 'Unstructured' is a wrong reading, so this is a mismatch with the PATO meaning.
The tip of the lamina is the bearer, but the examples describe a toothed margin near the apex. The bearer should be the margin.
A leaf base can be winged.
An ovary can be rhomboid in shape.
A corolla lip can be thin in thickness. The example 'lip attached to apex of column foot, thin' should be checked.
Pedicels can be lax.
Infrastaminal scales have a 2-D shape (ovate, oblong, spatulate).
A gynophore can be obsolete or vestigial.
Inflorescence bracts can be spreading.
Ray flowers can be stiff or rigid.
A leaf apex can be involute (rolled inward).
Anther thecae can be spreading or divergent.
A moss peristome can be split into segments.
A fruit pedicel can be pubescent.

The examples are comparisons ('wider than'), and the PATO term is a comparative modifier, not a quality of the leaf. A comparison should be handled by a rule for the compared width, not a leaf quality.
Tepals can be coriaceous (leathery).
